title: Proposal for formDisabledCallback, formAssociatedCallback, and moveBefore() + FACE interaction

labels.name: topic: custom elements
labels.description: Relates to custom elements (as defined in DOM and HTML)

labels.name: interop
labels.description: Implementations are not interoperable with each other

body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

As discussed in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12169 (cc @Lubrsi) and somewhat in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/8365, there is no normative specification text for when `formDisabledCallback` and `formAssociatedCallback` fire. (Except for the upgrades case.) While implementing these parts of the spec in jsdom, I found that browsers have interop issues here, mainly around cases like "moving a custom element from one form to another in a way that changes its disabled state". Furthermore, when combined with `moveBefore()`, browsers have some bizarre results that seem like bugs, although they are interoperable.

GPT-6 Astra Extra High has drafted a proposal ([HTML branch](https://github.com/whatwg/html/compare/main...codex/form-control-dom-hooks), [DOM branch](https://github.com/whatwg/dom/compare/main...domenic:codex/connection-reactions-before-hooks), [WPT branch](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/compare/master...codex/form-control-mutation-reactions)), but the changes are extensive enough, and in the `moveBefore()` cases do not match existing browsers. So, I wanted to get a discussion going before submitting.

All of the text in this issue is human-written, except for some copy-pasted tables and code-samples.

## Simple, no-`moveBefore()` cases

### Case 1: Ordinary insertion into and removal from a disabled fieldset

```html
<form id="A"><fieldset disabled></fieldset></form>
<script>
// Assume x-control is a FACE
const c = document.createElement("x-control");
document.querySelector("fieldset").append(c);
// Clear the callback log, then:
c.remove();
</script>
```

| Engine | Insertion | Removal |
|---|---|---|
| Chromium | connected → associated(A) → disabled(true) | disconnected → associated(null) → disabled(false) |
| Firefox | connected → associated(A) → disabled(true) | associated(null) → disconnected → disabled(false) |
| WebKit | connected → disabled(true) → associated(A) | disconnected → disabled(false) → associated(null) |

I think there are two reasonable possibilities here:

- "Most fundamental" first, both insertion and removal: Chromium matches this
- "Most fundamental" first on insertion, reverse on removal: nobody matches this

Therefore I propose we adopt Chromium's behavior here.

**Adopting Chromium's behavior here requires somewhat invasive DOM Standard changes**, since right now, the DOM Standard always does insertion steps and then `connectedCallback`, or removing steps and then `disconnectedCallback`. The ordering needs to be reversed, so that we can enqueue `connectedCallback`/`disconnectedCallback` first, and then use the insertion steps/removing steps to enqueue the other callbacks.

### Case 2: attribute changes

A simple case: doing `c.setAttribute("disabled", "")` on an initially-enabled FACE.

| Engines | Order |
|---|---|
| Chromium / Firefox | attributeChanged(disabled) → disabled(true) |
| WebKit | disabled(true) → attributeChanged(disabled) |

I propose we adopt the majority behavior here. This fits with the DOM Standard's existing arrangement of enqueing `attributeChangedCallback` before running the attribute change steps (which would be where we enqueue the `formDisabledCallback`)

### Case 3: upgrades

<details>
<summary>Collapsed by default since this is just a Chromium bug, the spec is fine</summary>

```html
<form id="A"><x-control disabled></x-control></form>
<script>
// Register x-control as FACE
</script>
```

| Engines | Order |
|---|---|
| Chromium | attributeChanged(disabled) → connected → disabled(true) → associated(A) |
| Firefox / WebKit | attributeChanged(disabled) → connected → associated(A) → disabled(true) |

This case is actually already specced; [upgrades are the only places that normatively queue the two callbacks](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/custom-elements.html#concept-upgrade-an-element).

</details>

WPT here, someone please approve them: https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/64693

## Enter `moveBefore()`

### Simple `moveBefore()` case

The basic problem is that, contrary to the spirit of `moveBefore()`, Chromium and Firefox (WebKit doesn't implement `moveBefore()`) seem to temporarily disassociate form controls during a move, which can also flip their disabled state. This doesn't make a lot of sense.

```html
<form id="A">
  <fieldset disabled><x-control id="c"></x-control></fieldset>
</form>
<form id="B"><fieldset id="destination" disabled></fieldset></form>
<script>
const c = document.getElementById("c");
const destination = document.getElementById("destination");
destination.moveBefore(c, null);
</script>
```

Chromium and Firefox both give: associated(null) → disabled(false) → connectedMove → associated(B) → disabled(true)

**Proposed behavior**: connectedMove → associated(B). This seems more in line with how moving is supposed to work: instead of going from A → null → B, the control goes straight from A → B. And since the control stays disabled before and after, nothing changes.

### Moving a legend

This is a tricky edge case. [The descendants of a disabled `<fieldset>`'s *first* `<legend>` are not themselves disabled](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-elements.html#attr-fieldset-disabled). So watch this.

```html
<form id="A"><fieldset disabled>
  <legend id="moving"><x-control></x-control></legend>
</fieldset></form>
<form id="B"><fieldset id="destination" disabled>
  <legend></legend>
</fieldset></form>
<script>
document.getElementById("destination").moveBefore(
  document.getElementById("moving"), null
);
</script>
```

| Approach | Order |
|---|---|
| Chromium / Firefox | associated(null) → connectedMove → associated(B) → disabled(true) |
| My draft | connectedMove → associated(B) → disabled(true) |
| Simpler single-pass alternative | disabled(true) → connectedMove → associated(B) |

To explain: my draft, linked above, tries to maintain the semantic of "most fundamental first" mentioned in case 1. However, to do this in this kind of case, we need a bit of extra machinery. I think it's probably fine? But I wanted to put it out there.

The simpler single-pass alternative queues each node's connection reaction immediately before its own moving steps. The ancestor legend’' steps can therefore queue the control's disabledness reaction before traversal reaches the control.
